ELi5: Why does caffeine wake us up/make us hyper?

Nerdy Copy Pasta;

To a nerve cell, caffeine looks like adenosine. Caffeine binds to the adenosine receptors. However, in contrast to adenosine, it does not decrease the cell's activity. As caffeine utilizes all the receptors adenosine binds to, the cells can no longer sense adenosine. As a result, instead of slowing down because of the adenosine level, the cells speedup.

Caffeine blocks adenosine's ability to open up the brain's blood vessels, causing them to constrict - this is the reason caffeine is used in pain reliever medicine for headaches. If the headache is vascular, the caffeine closes down the blood vessels and gives relief.

With caffeine blocking adenosine, there is an increase in the firing of neurons in the brain. The pituitary gland observes the increased activity and perceives it as an emergency, so it releases hormones that tell the adrenal glands to produce adrenaline (epinephrine). I see this term thrown around quite often by the right-leaning people here and I'd like to have a little discourse on its usage so we can have a more clear discussion.

First off, what most people are referring to when they mean "state religion" or other forms of socialism is closest actually to Feuerbach and his conception. Feuerbach essentially argued that Christianity was just anthropology, but we could replace God with socialism and come to a humanist, secular utopia.

Now, Feuerbach was a Hegelian which means not much for this discussion except that he believe ideas moved history. Essentially, the belief is that feudalism was a result of the shifting of intellectual perspectives, not the result of material conditions.

This is where Marx made his first drastic movement. Dialectical materialism just means, instead of seeing history as the movement of ideas, the movement of history was rather the material conditions formed by class struggle, and ideas of any time reflect material conditions.

Marx's primary work was economics. So why's he associated with communist revolution? Marx never once gave a moralistic criticism of capitalism, rather, he saw it as the greatest development in history so far, as it gave people access to a wide variety of new innovations and choices very rapidly. Instead, he believed a non-organized proletariat uprising would one day lead a charge into a new era. So basically what this means is, when you see educated liberals trying to organize revolution, or arguing for it, you're not seeing orthodox Marxism. This is closer rather to Bolshevism, or Marxist-Leninism, which is an adaption of Marx's economics with Lenin's ideas for instigating global revolution.

I'll add here an important note about Marx's theory of revolution: Marx believed that, in the proletariat-led revolution, morality would be unnecessary. Marx believed morality was a bourgeoise concern and literally laughed at it. How can he justify this? Marx basically believed Rousseau: human nature is essentially good, and oppressive material conditions make him bad. Without class struggle, people would have no reason to hurt each other. It's easy to dismiss this outright, but most sociological studies do suggest that humans essentially work together, and tend not to confirm Hobbesian conceptions of human nature. Still, I find this to be the part of Marxism easiest to argue against.

So anyway, I see terms like "cultural Marxism" being used and I'm like.. what? If you believe Marxism is about forcing equality through a strong government, then my only impression is that you're ignorant about everything Marx said. I'd suggest the right-wingers here take the time to be more educated about so-called liberalism or Marxism before ranting against it.
